maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO EXTENT OF FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN ATLANTIC AREA

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO EXTENT OF FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN ATLANTIC AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the budget address on March 14 the Minister of Finance outlined a proposal that the government considered would be helpful in meeting the power requirements of the maritime provinces. Since that statement there have been a number of developments, and I think it might be of interest to hon. members to know something further about the proposal and where it now stands.
I will not repeat the statement by the Minister of Finance which can be found at page 2220 of Hansard for March 14. The same day it was made I wrote to Premier Stanfield and Premier Flemming enclosing a copy of it. I indicated that if they thought it would be desirable to have a meeting, either with me or on the official level, I would be very glad to arrange it.
I received an immediate reply from both premiers suggesting that a meeting of officials should be held. That meeting took place in Ottawa on March 21. A number of questions were discussed relating both to matters of policy and to details of application of the proposal. Following the report by the officials of the provincial power commissions to their
3294	HOUSE OF
Power Development-Atlantic Area respective premiers, I received telegrams from each premier accepting the federal proposal subject to discussion of further details. In the light of the discussions at the meeting of officials and of the acceptance by the premiers of the federal proposal, a number of further decisions have now been taken.
Hon. members will recall that at the last session of parliament an amendment to the Northwest Territories Power Commission Act was passed changing the name of the commission to the Northern Canada Power Commission and empowering it to acquire, operate and maintain power plants not only in the two territories but also in the provinces "with the approval of the governor in council but subject to the laws of the province in which the powers . . . are exercised".
It had not been thought at that time that the operations of the commission would ever extend to any part of Canada other than the territories or the northern limits of certain of the provinces. However, the legal position is that the commission can, with the approval of the governor in council and subject to the laws of the province concerned, operate in any province. The representatives of both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, but especially of the latter, raised considerations that gave urgency to the implementation of the federal proposal. In order to comply with the provincial desire that immediate action should be taken, the federal government has decided that the Northern Canada Power Commission should be designated as its agency to carry the proposals into effect. Order in council number 1957-476 was passed on April 4 for that purpose.
One of the matters of urgency is that the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission has prepared plans for the construction of a new plant of 50 megawatts capacity which the commission was intending to erect at Saint John. Tenders had actually been received when the statement of the Minister of Finance was made, although no contract for any part of the plant had been placed. The province of New Brunswick urged that this plant should be taken over under the federal proposal.
One question that was discussed at the meeting of officials was whether the construction of interconnection lines between the two provinces under the federal proposal might affect the urgency of the need for the plant or possibly might affect the determination of the most desirable location. It may be, for instance, that in order to serve an interconnected system covering the two provinces it would be more efficient to have a new plant in Cumberland county, Nova Scotia, to use coal from that area, rather than to have it in Saint John.


It has been decided that an immediate study should be undertaken to determine what new capacity may be required in the two provinces and, having regard to possible new interconnection lines, what would be the most effective and economic location. This study will be undertaken by the Montreal Engineering Company as consultants for the Northern Canada Power Commission. The study will be carried out in full consultation with the power commissions of the two provinces.
Pending the completion of this study, and in order that there may be no unnecessary delay in bringing a new power plant into operation at whatever location may be found most advantageous, the Northern Canada Power Commission has been authorized by the governor in council, under the order in council to which I have referred, to enter into the contract that the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission had planned to place for the turbo generator and other major equipment for the proposed 50,000 KW plant. It is expected that the contract will be placed within the next few days. As originally planned by the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, and as the delivery requirements of the contract will specify, this plant will be on a schedule that would call for delivery of power from it in 1959.
The studies to which I have referred of the required new capacity and of new interconnection lines are extensive and are not expected to be completed before August 1 of this year. The costs will be quite substantial. In the normal course, engineering studies undertaken by the Northern Canada Power Commission are charged, in accordance with section 14 of the act, against any project that results from the study. In order that there may be no undue burden of cost to be met out of the price charged for power in the maritimes, the government has decided that these studies that are now under way should be met by funds to be appropriated by parliament for that purpose. The submission of a suitable item will be made in due course for consideration by this house.
With regard to the fuel to be used by the plants that will be established under the federal proposal, the basic objective of securing power at the lowest possible cost is, of course, to be kept constantly in mind. This consideration will frequently affect the location of the plants that are to be built. It is, of course, also the desire of the government to see maritime coal used to the greatest extent possible in the plants that may be established. The sharp increase in the price

of oil and in charges for ocean shipping over recent months have resulted in a situation in which, over virtually all the maritime provinces, it appears that it would be cheaper to use maritime coal for the production of power than to use oil.
There is some reason to think that this increase in the price of oil may not be as temporary as has sometimes been hoped or suggested. In the circumstances, the economic advantage of the use of maritime coal shows every likelihood of continuing.
In the immediate future the first plant to be built by the Northern Canada Power Commission seems likely to be at Saint John or in Cumberland county. If it is in Cumberland county it will be because of the prospects of securing maximum economies through the use of coal from that area. If the best location turns out to be Saint John, the object will be to enter into arrangements with maritime coal producers so that coal may be used for fuel on a basis that will produce power at as low a cost as if oil were used. I have every confidence that such arrangements can be made. As I said at the outset, the object of the government in this proposal is to secure power at the lowest possible cost and at the same time to use maritime coal as the fuel for that purpose.
Contracts for the construction of plants and transmission lines to be built under the federal proposal will be placed on the basis of tenders to be called in each case; the same will apply to equipment. Contracts will be placed in the normal fashion with the lowest tenderer in a position to provide the quality of equipment and construction capacity that is required within whatever delivery schedule may be necessary. Design of plant and equipment required by the Northern Canada Power Commission will normally be undertaken by it, through its consulting engineers, unless in any particular case a special arrangement is made. Such a special arrangement might apply, for instance, to projects like the Saint John plant, which are already in the course of design and which are to be taken over by the federal agency. Naturally, all questions relating to the capacity and character of facilities will be a matter for consultation with the provincial power commissions.
The plants will be operated by the Northern Canada Power Commission with the power sold at cost to the agency designated by the province. The same cost basis will apply to the rental of transmission lines. Rental of these lines will provide for maintenance to be undertaken by the lessee.
The financing of plants and transmission lines will be in accordance with the normal 82715-208i
9. 1957	3295
Power Development-Atlantic Area financing of construction undertaken by the Northern Canada Power Commission, that is at the federal borrowing rate plus a small additional charge that is normally made for the provision of finances to crown corporations. Amortization of the thermal plants will be over the 30-year period which is normal for such plants, and the steel tower high voltage interconnection lines will be over the 40-year period which is normal for them.
As has been indicated throughout, the principal purpose behind the proposal of the government is to supply power in the maritime provinces on the most efficient basis possible and at the lowest possible cost. There will, of course, have to be an agreement with the governments of the maritime provinces with regard to the proposal generally, and also with regard to the specific plants and interconnection lines. In accordance with the underlying purpose of the project, a provision of all agreements will be one requiring the provincial governments under their normal powers of regulation, or through the establishment of charges by their respective power commissions, to see that the benefits of reduced power costs are passed on to the consumers. The provincial power commissions, or in some cases private utilities, will be in a position to buy power from the Northern Canada Power Commission at a favourable rate, and they will be expected to see-I have no doubt they will be anxious to see-that the full benefit goes to the industrial or domestic users.
It is my belief, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal that has been put forward, and which has been so promptly accepted by the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, will operate to the genuine advantage of the maritime provinces.

Last week the hon. member for Oxford inquired with respect to the conditions of service of Canadian forces in the Middle East. He based his question on a newspaper report which in turn referred to alleged remarks by a member of the Canadian contingent who had recently returned to Canada. The gist of these remarks was that Canadian troops were so discontented with conditions in Egypt that some of them were purposely getting into trouble in order to be sent home.
As I pointed out to the hon. member on Friday, this appeared to be completely at variance not only with the information we ourselves had received but also with dispatches being sent by newspaper reporters from the area. For this reason I asked for a full report direct from the Middle East.
I have now received this report, and I may say that it confirms entirely my original understanding of the situation existing there. I can now say that since the arrival of the contingent only two members of the force have been returned to Canada for disciplinary

Inquiries of the Ministry reasons, and there is nothing to indicate that their offences were committed with this end in view. As a matter of fact, the incidence of crime in the contingent is somewhat lower than in the army as a whole.
None of us would contend, Mr. Speaker, that conditions in Egypt and the Gaza strip are ideal. The Canadian units of UNEF are operating under field conditions in an area which has recently been the scene of warfare. While accommodation and welfare arrangements cannot come up to the standards in Canada, they are the best obtainable under the circumstances. I think the majority of our men realize this and I am confident that, despite the conditions, their morale and conduct are extremely good. In fact General Burns himself has indicated very definitely that the conduct of our troops in UNEF is a credit to them and to Canada.

The aircraft crashed about six minutes after nine p.m., within a few minutes of the last radio contact with Uplands, at which time there was no reason to believe that the pilot was experiencing any difficulty.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO MOVING SUPPLY MOTION
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion provides the opportunity to bring before the
3302	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Support Prices house matters of national interest. On this occasion I propose to deal in general with the subject of agriculture and the need for action to be taken in order to provide and assure that the farmer shall have a fair and reasonable share of the national income.
I do not intend to deal with marketing legislation in any way, though ordinarily I would have done so. However, I express the hope that tomorrow the legislation that was introduced yesterday will be brought before the house, and that no excuse will be offered for not having it passed at the present session. We are most desirous of that being done. I mention that point merely in passing, namely that no excuse will be accepted by the opposition for any action that might be taken to delay the further processing of that bill and its enactment at the present session.
I commence by saying what has been said on previous occasions, namely that the farmer finds himself squeezed between rising costs of production and falling farm prices. His position is that he gets less and pays more. While there has been some improvement in the matter of the net national farm income within recent months, none the less the fact remains to be emphasized that the farmer still finds himself in a difficult and, in my opinion, perilous position.
The general submission of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made on December 3 last to the federal-provincial agricultural conference sets out the facts in general. I shall do no more than refer to one or two matters stated in that submission, instead of plastering the record with a great number of statistics to support the conclusions of that body. The submission states:
Farm prices in 1956 have been 6 per cent lower than in 1949, while costs of goods and services the farmer buys have increased 20 per cent.
Then it adds these words:
This means that the farmers' unfavourable price position is caused more by extraordinary increase in costs, than by the fall in farm price levels.
Then at page 3 of that submission there are set out in detail the changes that have taken place in recent years in Canadian agriculture, and in particular that during a period of ten years the number of farms dropped from 695,000 to 531,000, a drop of 24 per cent.
Indeed, on reading this summary we find that the general picture is such that Canadian agriculture finds itself in a difficult and trying position, which is not met by the quoting of statistics designed to show that there is statistical prosperity within our country.
It deals in particular with poultry prices and with the turkey producer's position. That
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

producer finds himself with depressed prices resulting in considerable measure from unjustified competition on the part of United States producers. The fruit and vegetable farmers also find that United States farm products of this kind are being dumped into Canada, and that today there is no protection by way of anti-dumping duties or tariffs. Action must be taken in order to assure that valuation shall be properly determined, but not on the basis of invoices from the United States of America.
Then also the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a full submission to the Prime Minister and the members of the cabinet on February 15 of this year. I shall do no more than quote one or two of the representations epitomizing, as they do, the situation that prevails. On page 1 they state:
Farmers from coast to coast feel keenly that on the average their returns have become badly out of balance with those of other major groups in the nation. It is important to emphasize purchasing power in this connection because the farmers' difficulties are to be found as much in high prices of the things he buys as in a decline in the number of dollars he receives.
Then it deals in particular with the price support legislation and endeavours to show- and I think successfully-that as this policy of the government in connection with agricultural price support has been revealed year by year, and as over the years the policy and philosophy of the government in administering this act has developed, it has been used only in the case of extreme price decline, in circumstances where the cost to the government will be moderate and the possibility of creating any real problems in the field of surplus disposal and trade relations would be almost entirely avoided. In other words, to summarize what has been represented by this great national farm organization the returns of farmers are out of balance with those of other major groups in the nation, and unless agriculture is stabilized and balanced the entire Canadian economy will suffer in consequence.
I believe that the two major objectives that must be faced by parliament are to assure stability for the farmer and also, as I mentioned a moment ago, to assure him a fair and reasonable share of the national income. The farmer finds himself in the position where his markets have been lost or diminished because of ineffective trade policies of the federal government. Briefs have been presented year by year by representative farm organizations, but the farmer finds himself gradually achieving a position detrimental to the preservation of the Canadian agricultural production machine.

Then also there is another phase that must be considered, for it reverses in Canada the trend in United States of America. The farmer's share of the consumer's dollar has been reduced considerably in recent years.
About 10 years ago the farmer's share was 59 cents, while today it is just about 50 cents. In spite of an increase in actual production since 1951, the farmer more and more is receiving less and less than a fair percentage of the total annual product.
It is no answer to say that in 1956 the share of Canadian agriculture began to approximate, to a degree that had not been so in preceding years, the net income of 1951, for the reason that the net national product of Canada in th._ same period has very materially increased, and as a result the disparity on the part of agriculture has increased and its share has decreased.
This is not a problem that affects only the farmers. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in one of their briefs, have set out in detail the farmers' problems. They point out that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce recognizes that a sound and prosperous agriculture is vital to Canada's economy; that the interests of the agricultural industry and labour are interdependent, and the chamber therefore makes recommendations in detail as to the action that must be taken in order to preserve and increase agriculture's share of the gross national product. To those who object to farmers engaging in the marketing of their own products it is of interest to note that in recent representations made by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce these words appear:
The chamber recognizes the right of producers of farm products to act together with respect to the sale of their own products. The freedom of farmers to organize and seek a sound solution to the problem of marketing is part of our Canadian way of life.
I mention that because there are some who would lead people to believe that business in this country is opposed to co-operative farm organizations.
I mentioned a moment ago that one of the difficulties in which farmers find themselves today is the vast importation of farm products that is taking place in this country. The farmer finds himself handicapped by the failure of the government to act effectively regarding the imports of farm products, many of which seem to be dumped on the Canadian market and have a detrimental effect on the Canadian farmers' market. On the other hand the United States has followed the course of permitting the import of Canadian farm products into that country, but 82715-209J
Agricultural Products-Support Prices whenever these importations have a detrimental effect on United States farmers, immediately Canada finds its imports under quota or restricted.
It is of interest to note that we on this side of the house, and particularly members from the maritimes such as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) and all Conservative members from the maritimes, have pointed out the situation with regard to potatoes. No action was taken until April 5, 1957. As I listened today to the revelation of what is contemplated in connection with power in the maritimes I could not but think of the remarkable impetus the re-election of one Conservative government in New Brunswick and the election of a new Conservative government in Nova Scotia have had on the thinking of this government which for so long has refused to act. If we could have an election every year there would certainly be beneficial results in various parts of this country which have been lacking for so many years.

subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO MOVING SUPPLY MOTION

speechtext: We might even get something in Ontario.

subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO MOVING SUPPLY MOTION
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
Agricultural Products-Support Prices into Canada. I say that advisedly, because at the present time valuations are accepted on the basis of the invoice price. Unless a change is made in that regard and valuations based on fair market values are applied, the Canadian farmer will find himself very detrimentally affected. I refer particularly at the moment to the fruit farmers of this country. Indeed, Canadian markets are being flooded with United States potatoes, fruits and vegetables, because the United States can produce and ship its very high volume surplus and undersell Canadian competition. We find that one of the companies today is able to package goods-it is a company that operates in Canada as well-and send them to Canada, and the Canadian company cannot meet the competition of its own products. The Canadian canning companies, particularly the small ones, are faced with competition they cannot meet, with large foreign companies coming into Canada and seeming to operate without *egard to losses.
I mentioned some of the imports into Canada. I am going to summarize just a few. I find that in 1952 the importations of fruit, fresh, dried and canned, and fruit juices and syrups amounted to $99,761,000. In 1956 that amount increased to $121 million. Vegetable imports increased in the same period from approximately $41 million to some $50 million in 1956; poultry, fowl and turkeys from $290,000 in 1952 to $5,556,000 in 1956. Canned peaches-and this tells the story-imported from the United States in 11 months of 1956, the latest figures I have available, came to 8,614,000 pounds and canned fruits other than peaches amounted to 32,170,000 pounds.
This is a serious situation. We want trade, but we do not want Canada's agricultural producers challenged by unfair competition brought about by the dumping of farm products into Canada. The Canadian Horticultural Council, in its recommendations to the cabinet on February 14, said this:
It is doubtful if, at any time in the past, our primary producers of fruits and vegetables have been so exercised or have suffered such serious losses as during the past years, from the "dumping" of like products from the United States on the Canadian market. These products may not be "dumped" within the limited definition of that term in the Customs Act or the Customs Tariff Act, but the effects on the financial returns of the Canadian farmer are just the same as though they had been "dumped" within the definition of the legislation.
That, in general, represents the views of the horticultural council. It says that approximately 50 per cent by value of all exports to Canada of fresh fruits and vegetables enter duty free. Much of these free products are citrus fruits, pineapples, melons

and grapes, and they compete, of course, with Canadian fruits. Substantial concessions were made to the United States or to the interests of the United States effective June 30, 1956, on certain fruit juices, processed pineapples, cherries and other processed horticultural products, all of which compete with Canadian products, but for which-and this I underline-there is no compensating concession on Canadian horticultural products.
That situation is detrimental and serious to Canada. The agreements on tariffs and trade have not been lived up to by the United States. They have been lived up to by Canada, but in so far as the United States is concerned it has almost with impunity broken those agreements in connection with agricultural products, which very seriously affects the Canadian economy.
As far as the wheat markets are concerned, they have been undermined by the unlawful give-away programs of the United States which have caused patent injustices to Canada. I believe the time has come to say a word to the United States, a word that can be understood, that we Canadians object most strenuously to policies that are in derogation of the general agreement on tariffs and trade and to the detriment of the Canadian farmer.
Take flour, for instance, as a good example. The United States has a subsidy on wheat of $1.84 per hundredweight. I worked it out on the basis of a hundredweight. Its flour subsidy is $2.34 per hundredweight. In other words United States millers receive an extra subsidy of 50 cents per hundredweight on all wheat exported in the form of flour. The Canadian subsidy, which was introduced recently, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said would do something to meet this situation created by Canadian orders for flour being filled not in Canada from Canadian wheat, but in the United States from United States wheat bagged as though it were Canadian flour, with the export orders filled in a manner detrimental to us. The United States gives its flour millers a subsidy of 37J cents per hundredweight more than the Canadian government. Both wheats are approximately competitively priced in the export market. Our Canadian mills cannot compete with the current subsidy of 5J cents a bushel out of Atlantic ports.
We are losing our markets for flour because of effective action being taken by the United States and little action being taken by Canada. I believe if Canada wants to meet the situation it will have to increase the subsidy on flour so that Canada again may

start exporting in volume, and when she does our surpluses of wheat will be reduced.
Some ask, what about the cost in that connection? Well, I point out that when the wheat is kept in storage it costs the wheat board 20 cents per bushel per year, and if an extra subsidy were given on flour it would bring about savings in storage; it would stimulate Canadian production and would reduce, to the degree to which flour production was encouraged, our surpluses.
I mentioned, sir, the question of the Agricultural Prices Support Act; that a policy has developed that is used only in extreme circumstances, and that its present uses are not providing the necessary floors to maintain a responsible, profitable agriculture. We believe that a maximum of stability of income must be assured; that it is basic to Canada that the preservation of the agricultural machine shall be assured, and that having regard to the present use of floor prices under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, the producers of eggs, chickens and turkeys as well should be assured of a reasonable floor under their products.
Throughout the years we in this party have advocated that action be taken on behalf of the farmer, and I am going to set out in detail some of the suggestions we have made and the motions we have moved in order to answer the propaganda that is sometimes spread that the Conservative party has no interest in the welfare of the farmer. I go back to April 8, 1941, as reported in Hansard at page 2280 when, on a similar occasion on a motion to go into supply I had the honour to move, seconded by Mr. Gordon Graydon:
That the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agriculture and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture in order that it may receive a just and fair return.
Then on March 23, 1953, I moved on behalf of this party, as reported at page 3208 of Hansard:
In the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.
Then on March 12, 1956, as reported at page 2026 of Hansard of that date, I moved on behalf of this party, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
That ... in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.
That has been our stand and it will continue to be our stand, although there has been misinterpretation of a stand we took
9, 1957	3305
Agricultural Products-Support Prices in January last. At that time, in keeping with our responsibilities and realizing that the motion that had been introduced could not be effectuated and indeed was suspect, we refused to give it our support. It was meaningless and designed to confuse and deceive, because it held out promises that could not be carried into effect. It denied the need of flexible floor prices and promised 100 per cent income, without in any way indicating what would be par in connection with such an income.
In other words through the years we have endeavoured to assure the farmer of a fair share of the national income. Our objective is the equality of farmers in Canada's economy. We believe that action must be taken to correct the social inequity and the inferior economic position into which agriculture has been allowed to fall. We believe that action must be taken and taken at once.
One has just to look at the purchasing power of the dollar to realize the situation in which the farmer finds himself in relation to the prices which are paid today for Canadian farm products. With regard to all cost of living items, if the dollar had a purchasing power of $1 in 1939, in January, 1957, it had shrunk to 53 cents. The food dollar with a purchasing power of $1 in 1939, in January, 1957, had a purchasing power of 45 cents. The shelter dollar has a purchasing power of 63 cents today. The rent dollar has a purchasing power of 62 cents, and the clothing dollar a purchasing power of 51 cents today.
Those percentages indicate the degree to which the dollar has depreciated. Farm prices, whatever their comparison may be with those that existed in the past, are lower in purchasing power than they have been at any time since 1931 and 1932, at the height of the world depression. At that time prices in every part of the world fell to rock bottom levels because of the world depression that affected all; yet today Canadian farm prices have depreciated to a degree that is comparable in terms of purchasing power only to the worst days of the world-wide depression.
We believe that action must be taken now. I have already mentioned the Agricultural Products Marketing Act. That is now before the house, and it has received and will receive our support in order to enable farmers to market their products in a democratic and orderly manner. We believe that action must also be taken to recover our lost and diminished markets, particularly the British market for agricultural products. In keeping with our conviction we have advocated and pressed for a British commonwealth trade conference so that farm product and other markets may be developed and expanded in
3306	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Support Prices the commonwealth; but for some reason the members supporting the government have voted on every occasion against this demand and the motions I mentioned regarding farm prices.
We believe the time has come to investigate the very wide disparity between the price the farmer receives and the price paid by the consumer, as I pointed out a moment ago. We believe that the agricultural committee could have done a worth-while work in that connection had it been given the opportunity. Certainly it did not take the Minister of Agriculture very long to clear up the recent situation in connection with sheep. On that occasion he went into action quickly. Similar prompt action on the part of the government in convening the agricultural committee to investigate the disparity in the share the farmer receives of the ultimate consumer dollar would have paid dividends to the farmer.
We have repeated over and over again our belief that Canada should not stand idly by while its wheat markets are being lost through policies of the United States which are not fair or recognized competition but are actually policies that provide prices against which we cannot compete. These policies, as I said before, are contrary to the agreements that are in effect among the free nations of the world.
We believe, too, that action must be taken for the enactment of permanent floor price legislation based on a definite formula to allow for variations in production and demand for individual products. It is our contention that such floor prices should be announced well in advance of the production period each year and after consultation with representative producers and agricultural organization. We believe that a flexible price support program is the only means that will ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers based on a fair price cost relationship. We hold the view that only by action such as this will be met the problem which the agricultural industry faces today of falling prices and increasing costs of production.
The farmer is caught in that ruthless squeeze. At the present time the problem has not been met nor has any effective action been taken to preserve and maintain the integrity of agriculture against the adverse effects of that squeeze. For that reason we in this party believe that action should be taken now, and I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
[Mr. DiefenbakerJ

That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to introducing during the present session of parliament legislation which will assure farmers support prices for agricultural products based on a fair price-cost relationship, thereby resulting in agriculture receiving its reasonable share of the national income."

subtopic: PROCEDURE WITH RESPECT TO MOVING SUPPLY MOTION

speechtext:
It looks as if I have the
floor now. This is not an easy matter to decide. The amendment which was moved by the Leader of the Opposition reads as follows:
In the opinion of this house consideration should be given to introducing during the present session of parliament legislation which will assure farmers support prices for agricultural products based on a fair price-cost relationship, thereby resulting in agriculture receiving its reasonable share of the national income.
It has been contended that the terms of this amendment are similar to the terms of other amendments moved in the course of the present session, and that therefore citation 332 of Beauchesne's third edition should govern. This citation reads:
It is a rule in both houses, which is essential to the due performance of their duties, that no question or bill shall be offered that is substantially the same as one on which their judgment has already been expressed in the current session.
What are the other amendments that have been offered which it is claimed were in similar terms to the one moved today by the Leader of the Opposition? It has been said that there was one moved on January 23 by the hon. member for Yorkton and which reads as follows:
We regret, however, that Your Excellency's advisers seem to favour a flexible price support program, the effect of which is to leave the


agricultural industry in a state of uncertainty and insecurity; we also regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take the necessary steps to establish a system of parity prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure 100 per cent parity of income for agricultural producers.
It has been advanced further that the subject matter of the amendment moved today by the Leader of the Opposition was included in the terms of a subamendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer on January 17 and the vote on which appears in the Journals on page 61. This subamendment reads as follows:
-and, by reason of their failure to take effective action to stop the continuous rise in the cost of living; their failure to lay down and follow policies under which Canadian farmers and other primary producers can enjoy an equitable share of the prosperity which Canada can achieve; and their failure to bring old age pensions and other social security payments into line with the present cost of living.
Perhaps I should point out also that on the motion to go into committee of ways and means for the purpose of the presentation of the budget the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) moved an amendment on behalf of the official opposition as recorded at page 2469 of Hansard for March 19, 1957, subparagraph (d) of which reads:
(d) ignores the problems and needs of agriculture.
The general paragraph of that amendment was an follows:
This house regrets that the economic policy of the government fails, despite a very large surplus, to meet the needs of the Canadian people and in particular-
Then follow paragraphs (a) (b) (c), and then (d) which reads:
-ignores the problems and needs of agriculture.
It would appear that we are now being faced with the consequences of wide amendments being moved to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, to supply motions when they are presented to be debated, and also to the motion to go into committee of ways and means for the purpose of the presentation of the budget. I have already pointed out to the house that difficulties may ensue from the moving of omnibus amendments to these various questions which provide the house with opportunities for moving want of confidence motions.
If I had, since the beginning of this session, adhered strictly to the rules as they are laid down, it would have been my duty to declare out of order motions which were moved previously. By examining these various amendments one can easily see the wide amendment that was moved in reply to the speech from the throne, and that the various

I did not declare some of those amendments out of order because I took it the house would agree with me that these opportunities, which are opposition opportunities to move want of confidence motions, offer great latitude. Mr. Speaker, I do not like to thresh old straw but, as I said before lunch, in debating this amendment I am going to have to reiterate the same old arguments that have been used on other occasions during this session when we debated similar amendments.
I am not going to take exception to the figures placed on the record by the Leader of the Opposition. He mentioned today that the costs of agricultural producers in this country had increased by 20 per cent. He also pointed out that the share of the national income which is going to agriculture today has dropped to 6 per cent. As a matter of fact, I think it is fair to say that in the last 10 years the share of the national income going to agricultural producers in this country has dropped from something in the neighbourhood of 11 per cent to something in the neighbourhood of 5.6 per cent. I would go even further and say that since 1951 the net farm income in western Canada has dropped by 66g per cent.
There has certainly been some increase in farm cash income in the last year or so, in the last year in particular; but I contend, sir, that farm net income is still declining. To substantiate that statement I wish to refer the house to the report of the Saskatchewan wheat pool in which we find that the average price the farmers in western Canada can expect to receive from the sale of their wheat for last year will be $1.29 per bushel f.o.b. Fort William.
When you consider that because of the cost-price squeeze, and the unfair relationship between the farmer's cost of production on the one hand and the price he receives for his produce on the other, you readily realize that today the farmer is attempting to operate with a 45-cent dollar. Certainly that gives some appreciation of the problem that agricultural producers in this country are experiencing.
I believe it is fair to say that of all industries in this country, agriculture is the most depressed at the present time. During the past few years the government has brought in a great many measures in an effort to alleviate the problem of agriculture but they see it as a local problem and fail to recognize


that the problem of agriculture is national. If it is going to be solved it must be solved on a national basis. The government must recognize the problem of agriculture as a national problem.
The treatment the agricultural producer is receiving today is somewhat different and a trifle removed from the treatment this government is according to practically every industry in this country with the exception of agriculture. To illustrate my point I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the position of one of the leading branches of a Canadian industry. I wish to put on the record a description of the position of Canada Packers Limited, in order that we may compare it with the position occupied by the agricultural industry, because of the different treatment that has been accorded it.
I have here a list of figures showing the capital investment and the profit on the capital investment of Canada Packers Limited, a relatively small part of one industry with capital investment assets of something in the neighbourhood of $30,750,000. The figures contained in the annual report of Canada Packers Limited show an average profit for ten years of 27J per cent on their capital investment. This is more than three times the expected return on general capital investment, and 25 times more than was received by farmers on their capital investment in 1954.
I have just pointed out that the capital investment of Canada Packers Limited is $30,750,000, yet the capital investment of Canadian agriculture is in excess of $10 billion, so there we have a picture of the kind of treatment that is accorded to one industry in this country as compared to another. I submit, sir, that what has been accomplished by Canada Packers Limited is a fair illustration of what is being accomplished by every other industry in this country with the exception of agriculture.
I have said that measures must be taken that have not yet been taken to date to grapple with this problem. There must be recognition of the over-all problem of agriculture. The time has come when we must stop trying to solve the agricultural problem in this country by the implementation of a series of ad hoc pieces of legislation. Unless we do something by way of introducing a comprehensive agricultural policy in this country the agricultural industry is headed for bankruptcy.
We in this party stand foursquare for a comprehensive agricultural policy based on the concept of parity prices, prices that bear a fair relationship to the cost of production on the one hand and the price received by

We are not even asking that the farmer be allowed to make a profit, nor are we suggesting, as the Canadian Pacific Railway are suggesting, that they should have the people of Canada subsidize them to the extent that they can show a profit on their capital investment of 4.71 per cent. We are simply suggesting that a parity price would be one that would bear a fair relationship to the costs and prices of a producer.
I am not carried away with the proposition of a two-price sytem. I think it is possible that we in Canada are going to have to accept a two-price system before we are going to get a comprehensive over-all policy of parity prices, but I think first of all we must establish the principle before we talk about the details.
There has been a lot of talk about deficiency payments. I am now speaking personally, for myself. As I say, I am not at all carried away with the proposition of deficiency payments on two counts. First of all, I think it is politically dishonest for anyone to go out land suggest that the people of Canada through the public treasury should pay the farmer a deficiency payment. That is a back door method of saying we are going to pay a subsidy. Why not be honest about it and say that the farmer deserves a parity price, one bearing a fair relationship to his costs and the price he receives for his products, rather than say, "We are going to pay you $1 a bushel for wheat. We know the parity price is $1.90, but by some back door method on a dark night in a back alley we are going to take out of the public treasury the difference between $1 and $1.90 and give it to you, and hope that we can get away with it without the people of Canada finding out about it".
I do not like that policy because I think it is politically dishonest. I am not worried that $2 a bushel is going to mean that the consumer in this country is going to pay more for the bread he buys.
Because it has been proved conclusively that if the price of wheat today were set at the parity price of $2.20 a bushel it would only raise the price of wheat by possibly three-quarters of a cent or 1 cent a loaf. As a matter of fact, statistics prove conclusively that if the farmer today gave his wheat to the millers for nothing it would lead to a reduction of only 3 cents in the cost of a loaf of bread. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am not too concerned about deficiency payments. I think, first of all, that it is politically dishonest, and I say that on my own account rather than for the party. That is one point to which I take exception.
The other point is this. I am not in favour of deficiency payments for the simple

Agricultural Products-Support Prices reason that I can see this pattern developing; a deficiency payment must be based on a fair price to the producer, and if the market is congested at a time when a farmer has a load of hogs or cattle what is to prevent a dealer coming to him and saying, "The market is not going to accept your produce today at the price you want for it. Sell it to me for a little less. You are going to get a deficiency payment anyway; why keep it on your hands?" Perhaps I am wrong, but at the moment I am not over concerned about fighting the case for deficiency payments. My proposition is this. Let us call spades, spades. Let us be honest. Deficiency payments, if they are made, are going to be based on prices, which are parity prices. So let us come out and say we are going to have a parity price.
Heaven knows we have a difficult job as it is in trying to sell to the people of eastern Canada-and perhaps it is understandable that they should think so-the proposition that interim and final payments from the Canadian wheat board are not subsidies paid out of the public treasury. We have not been able to sell even that proposition, let alone this proposition of deficiency payments as being nothing but a subsidy. Having said that, I want to add that we in this party stand foursquare on this concept and principle of a parity price.
What is a parity price? As far as I am concerned I shall be honest about it, and admit that it would be a very difficult task to say categorically what a parity price is; and I think any hon. member would be in the same difficulty. But my conception of a parity price, and the conception of a parity price which is held by the party which I represent, is not, for instance, a high support price on all the wheat we could grow in western Canada. That is not my conception, because I do not honestly think we can go on producing 400, 500 or 600 million bushels of wheat in this country and get away with it. I maintain that a parity price is a combination of a great many things. It means a system of crop insurance; it means a system of long and short-term credit; it means cash advances; it means marketing boards-

It means an extension of the marketing policies of the government; and all these things combined, I maintain, will give the farmer a parity price.
Hon. members have been talking about a parity price for wheat. I think we must face it that there is bound to be a reduction in the volume of a lot of things which are grown in this country. By that I do not


mean we shall need to curtail total production, but that we are going to have to curtail production in some directions; and I suggest we shall have to curtail the production of wheat.
A parity price will simply mean that people will be able to diversify their farming. A farmer who is now engaged strictly in wheat farming will be able to change the nature of his operation, something he cannot do at the present time because of the high cost such a change would involve. A farmer may be farming on marginal land which is, strictly speaking, not suitable for the production of wheat at all. That is the case with regard to a good deal of the land in my own area. I submit that we should not grow any wheat there at all, because we grow a wheat of low protein quality. Let the people down in Rosetown grow the wheat; they are the people who are in the best position to grow it. But there are other things we can grow better in the area where I live than anywhere else in Saskatchewan.
If I were to change my operation from a wheat operation to something else it would cost a lot of money, but if I knew I was going to get a parity price for what I produced as a result of the transfer of my operation to one which would be more efficient, I would do it and be glad to do it. Unless we do have a parity price system, however, which would encourage a farmer to switch his production to a more diversified type of agriculture, he would be a fool to do it before he received some assurance that at least his capital investment would be protected. There is not an industry in this country which would make a large capital investment unless it knew when the first soil was turned exactly how long it would take before the cost of the capital investment was recovered.
Mr. Speaker, I will say nothing further in that regard. I declare categorically that we stand foursquare for a comprehensive agricultural policy based on the principle of parity price, and we shall keep on fighting for the implementation of that policy. Mr. Speaker, it is becoming more and more difficult to speak on this subject without indulging in some form of repetition, because this is the fourth amendment we have had this session on the question of parity prices. For that reason I will speak at less length than I would normally do.

In speaking on agriculture I have always taken the stand on behalf of this group that we believe a sound long-term agricultural policy to be essential not merely for the welfare of the farmer but also for the welfare of the Canadian people and the people of the world at large. The only way people can be well fed is by agriculture maintaining its production at a high level, and when you consider that today 50 per cent of the world's population is undernourished it becomes evident that it is necessary for agriculture to remain efficient so we can produce an abundance of food.
We have taken the stand that sound agricultural policy requires support prices. We believe that those support prices should be given on the basis of a two-price system. We believe it is necessary to do everything in our power to expand markets, both domestic and external, and that we should have a system of all-risk crop insurance.
Let me come back to the question of support prices. We see a lot of criticism in eastern newspapers to the suggestion that the prices of farm products should be supported. You often read the statement in eastern newspapers that the farmers are always asking for a hand-out, and why should the farmers be guaranteed support prices? I maintain there is a very good reason why the farmers are justified in asking for support prices. I maintain that when the farmers ask for support prices they are not asking for a hand-out in any shape or form, but are merely asking the government to keep their end of a contract that was made in the latter years of the war.
It will be remembered that in the latter years of the war we had price ceilings on farm products along with price ceilings on other commodities, and that many farmers were very critical of the government when it placed ceilings on farm products. Why? For the very simple reason that during the depression years the farmers were told time and again that they could not expect the government to do anything about prices because farm prices were low internationally. They were told that it was a world situation, and therefore they would have to be satisfied to accept world prices even though they were low for their farm products. Yet very shortly after the declaration of war the farmers were told they could not have world prices. Prices had gone up and they were told that world prices were too high and they would have to take lower prices.
You cannot have it both ways. If the farmers have to take world prices when they are low they are entitled to world prices when they are high. They were denied that
Agricultural Products-Support Prices privilege in the latter years of the war, and it made it that much more difficult for farmers to pay off the debts incurred as the result of producing at depressed prices during the depression years. Farm organizations repeated what I have said to the government on various occasions, and the government finally told them that in return for accepting a ceiling on farm prices they would be guaranteed support prices as part of a permanent postwar policy. Many members on this side of the house have quoted from time to time the speech made by the former prime minister of the country in which he said that in return for the farmers accepting a ceiling on their products during the war they would be guaranteed support prices after the war, and as a sign of good faith the government brought in the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
We have heard a lot of discussion as to just what is meant by parity. Section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act does provide a form of parity. It says that the board will step in and buy farm products when the prices fall below the level of other products, and that they will endeavour to maintain prices of farm products at a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities. That is what is meant by parity in this case, a price that bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities.
Under the agricultural prices support board formula three years, 1943, 1944 and 1945, were established as the base period, and it was said that we would maintain the prices of farm products so today they would bear the same relationship to the prices of other commodities that existed in the three base years. When the farmers ask the government to live up to that formula they are merely asking the government to keep faith with the promise that was made at the end of the war; yet we find that today support prices are not on that basis but are well below it.
I have here a table I received from the agricultural prices support board dated January 11, 1957. In this table I note that the support price for butter is only 81 per cent of parity, based upon the years 1943, 1944 and 1945; that the support price of 23 cents for hogs is only 80 per cent of parity, and that the support price of 38 cents for eggs is only 54 per cent of parity.
Some suggestion has been made that 100 per cent of parity is too high, but this is merely 100 per cent of parity on the basis of the years 1943, 1944 and 1945. Is anybody going to suggest that during the years 1943, 1944 and 1945 the prices of agricultural products were too high compared with the prices of other commodities? I do not think

Agricultural Products-Support Prices anybody would dare say that, because at that time the prices of farm products were still fairly low by comparison. Therefore when we say today that prices of farm products should be maintained at 100 per cent of parity in relation to the years 1943, 1944 and 1945, all we are asking is that the same relationship should exist today between the prices of farm products and the prices of other commodities that existed in those years when price ceilings were in operation. Nobody would suggest for one minute that that would be unreasonable, and for anybody to suggest that the farmers should only get a percentage of that is to suggest that the farmers should only receive a percentage of a fair price instead of 100 per cent of a fair price.
Some people will say that the farmers have not done too badly. We continually hear people say that gross income is up, but gross income means nothing at all unless at the same time you take costs into consideration. If income goes up and costs go up at a greater rate than income, then the net income is going to be less. It is true that in 1957 there has been a slight improvement, but if we go back ten years what do we find was the situation?
The western pools presented a brief to the cabinet on March 9, 1957, which included tables showing prices of farm products and costs for the ten years from 1947 to 1956 inclusive. If anybody is in any doubt as to the condition of agriculture, let them peruse that brief. This is what it shows. Saskatchewan farm costs today are 45.9 per cent higher than they were ten years ago, while farm prices are 7.1 per cent lower than they were in 1947. What happened? For a few years after 1947 farm prices and farm costs rose pretty evenly, until approximately 1951. From 1951 onward farm costs continued to rise and farm prices started to fall with the result that comparing today with 1947 we find that farm costs have gone up over 45 per cent while farm income has dropped 7.1 per cent.
That, of course, is why the farmers are suffering from a cost-price squeeze. That is why I say most definitely that the government has not kept faith with the farmers. It has not kept the promise made by the then prime minister that if the farmers would agree to accept price ceilings the government in return would stabilize prices in the future. As I say, the government has not lived up to that promise.
I am sure anybody who is not familiar with parity prices will be very confused if they read Hansard of this session and the various motions that have been made. I would say

that anybody who is familiar with parity prices would be even more confused as to the stand of the Conservative party. If I am in order I should like to quote the different amendments that have been moved, to see if we can get some sense out of what they say and the action that has been taken with regard to them. On January 17 the hon. member for Red Deer moved an amendment in these words:
And, by reason of their failure to take effective action to stop the continuous rise in the cost of living; their failure to lay down and follow policies under which Canadian farmers and other primary producers can enjoy an equitable share of the prosperity which Canada can achieve . . .
That amendment received the support of the three opposition parties. Then on January 23 the hon. member for Yorkton moved an amendment in these words:
We regret, however, that Your Excellency's advisers seem to favour a flexible price support program, the effect of which is to leave the agricultural industry in a state of uncertainty and insecurity; we also regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take the necessary steps to establish a system of parity prices for agricultural producers at levels to ensure 100 per cent parity of income for agricultural producers.
Mind you, that was not to establish 100 per cent parity of price. It was merely to bring about 100 per cent parity of income. For reasons I still cannot understand the Conservatives voted against that proposition. If the motion had been for 100 per cent of parity price I could have understood it if they had voted against it. But the motion merely asked for 100 per cent of parity of income. Why should anybody say that the farmers of Canada are not entitled to their full share of the national income? In other words, as the farmers represent 15 per cent of the population, they should be entitled to 15 per cent of the income. Today the farmers are representing approximately 15 per cent of the population and they receive only 6.9 per cent of the income.
The C.C.F. motion was that they should receive 100 per cent of parity, and the Conservatives voted against it. For the life of me I cannot understand why they voted against it at that time, unless there was a misunderstanding. As I say, if the motion had been for 100 per cent of parity of price I could have understood it, because there might be times when you would say that in certain lines of production they should have less than parity and that in other lines of production they should have more than 100 per cent of parity, so that it would average 100 per cent of parity right across the industry but you would not maintain 100 per cent of parity in any one single line of production.

The present amendment reads as follows:
In the opinion of this house consideration should be given to introducing during the present session of parliament legislation which will assure farmers support prices for agricultural products based on a fair price-cost relationship, thereby resulting in agriculture receiving its reasonable share of the national income.
That word "reasonable" apparently means an amount less than parity, because the Conservative party voted against a parity of income. Hence they think the farmers should be satisfied with less than parity. The C.C.F. have tried to make the matter clearer by moving an amendment. I have not the amendment before me.

I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for handing me a copy. It reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom the words "its reasonable share of the national income" and by substituting therefor the following words: "a share of the national income based on parity".
That is common sense, Mr. Speaker. Now we know what we are talking about. I defy anybody to say what was meant by the amendment of the Conservative party. It could be anything that each individual member liked to make it. But one thing is clear, namely that it does not mean parity of income because they voted against it when it was before the house. We in this group believe that the farmers are entitled to their fair share of the national income, and that that should be 100 per cent of parity.
We did not consider that the agricultural prices support board, by using the years 1943, 1944 and 1945 as a basis, were establishing too high a basis. We thought that was a rather fair basis. I notice that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have suggested the years 1926 to 1929. But actually the base years 1943, 1944 and 1945 give a 1 per cent higher figure than do the base years suggested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I therefore think the agricultural prices support board and, to that extent, the government are to be congratulated upon using those three years as a basis for parity. I would criticize the government for not keeping their support prices at 100 per cent of the base years. As I pointed out, their support price is only approximately 80 per cent in the case of two products and only 54 per cent in the case of another. We in the Social Credit group have always taken the stand that support prices should be paid on the basis of a two-price system. We have taken that stand in this house ever since 1951.
I remember that the first time I became interested in the idea of a two-price system
Agricultural Products-Support Prices was when I attended a convention that was also attended by the Minister of Agriculture, namely the annual convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held at Niagara Falls. At that convention there was in attendance a professor from Harvard University; I refer to Professor Galbraith. He spoke about the two-price system. I thought it was a reasonable proposition. We in this group discussed it, and from then on we supported it. At that time it was not supported by the farm organizations, but about 1953 the interprovincial farm union took it up and supported the two-price system, and have supported it ever since. I remember that two years ago I was quite severely criticized by the hon. member for Assiniboia for advocating the two-price system. However, I am glad to note that the C.C.F. are broadminded on the question now. They do not oppose the two-price system. As a matter of fact I think they support it.
I believe the two-price system is a reasonable one. The two-price system merely says that farm products sold in the domestic market should be sold at parity and that farm products sold in the world market should be sold at the best prices that can be obtained, preferably under international agreement but supported at a reasonable level that will assure that the aggregate of the farmers' income will be on a parity with the income of other industries.
There is nothing new about the two-price system, nor is there anything unique about it. The secondary industries have always adopted the two-price system. They have always adopted a system of selling their commodities in the domestic market at a price that will bring them a fair return on their investment; then as to any surplus production they have had, they have sold it abroad for the best price they have been able to obtain. But just because they have had to sell their commodities in the world market at a certain price does not mean that they have sold their commodities in the domestic market at the same price. Very often the price at which they sold abroad was considerably lower than the price they charged in the domestic market.
As I say, the price they charge in the domestic market is a price that is necessary in order to bring them a fair return on their investment. That is very true of certain Canadian manufacturers of farm implements. I have priced machinery in England and I have priced it here; and I have found that they were selling machinery in England a great deal more cheaply than they were selling it in Canada at the time.
If it is good business for the secondary industries, why would it not be good business
3313	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Support Prices for agriculture? Of course the difference is that the secondary industries are in the position that they set the price, and they set the price at whatever level is necessary to give them a fair return on their investment. But agriculture has never been in a position to set its own price. The farmers take their commodities to market and are obliged to say, "What will you give us?" What do they get? They get approximately the same price as that for which those commodities sell on the world market.
Yet is it not a very strange situation when you take into consideration the fact that while 96 per cent or more of our farm products, excluding wheat, are sold in the domestic market, we nevertheless allow that 4 per cent which is exported abroad to set the price for the 96 per cent sold in Canada? In other words we are allowing the tail to wag the dog. Therefore those of us who advocate the two-price system for agriculture are only saying that the price for farm products in Canada should be at a level that bears a fair relationship, and nothing more, to the prices of other commodities; and then that the 4 per cent that is exported abroad should be sold at the best price we can obtain, preferably under international agreement such as we have under the international wheat agreement.
There is no doubt that it would be a great deal easier to operate the two-price system if we had all farm products sold under marketing boards, as is done by the wheat board. It would be a very simple matter then. But even without that advantage it would be possible to adopt the two-price system without boards by selling them on the weighted average between the price we get in the domestic market and the price we get abroad.
I have dealt with this subject at length on a number of occasions in this house; therefore I am not going to repeat my remarks now.
I will admit that it would be a whole lot easier to operate it if we had a system of marketing boards across the country. Not having the marketing boards, we could do it on the basis of estimating the amount of agricultural commodities that would be sold internally, the price we would sell them at internally at parity and estimating the amount we would sell abroad, the price we would get for them, and then pay the farmer a weighted average of those two prices. In that way, the two price system could be operated.
I have always felt though, in view of the definite commitment that was made by the Prime Minister at the end of the war, that


the government should live up to that commitment. The farmers, therefore, are absolutely justified in asking the government to maintain floor prices that will help to ensure farmers getting a parity of income on the basis of section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. It was for that reason some farm organizations asked a couple of years ago that wheat be brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Grain does not come under it. They wanted to have the assurance that there would be a support price under wheat in the same way as there is a support price under hogs, poultry, eggs and butter. At the present time all they have under wheat is the initial payment. As I have pointed out before, there is all the difference in the world between an initial payment and a support price. The purpose of a support price is to prevent the price from falling below a certain level at which the farmer would suffer a loss. An initial payment in the case of wheat is an estimate by the government of the price necessary in order to insure the government against suffering a loss. It was for that reason no doubt that on some occasions in the past when we have asked the government to notify us early in the year as to what the initial payment would be the minister has stated that he could not do it until he had a better idea what the price of wheat would be during the current year. He wanted to be certain there would be no losses entailed as a result of setting the initial payment too high. How could you possibly call that a support price? It is merely an estimate of what the lowest average price will be.
It is for that reason I feel the farmers are justified in asking that grain should be brought under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Then they could be guaranteed a support price which would return to the farmer a price that bore a fair relationship to the price of other commodities. If the price of wheat today were based upon the formula under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, that is a formula using the years 1943, 1944 and 1945 as base years, the price of wheat today would be $2.37 cents a bushel. I got that price in January from the bureau of statistics. What is the price the farmers are getting for wheat today? I notice that the wheat pools, in their brief to the government, show the average farm price is about $1.29, yet the support under the Agricultural Prices Support Act formula would be around $2.37 per bushel. They make this interesting comment regarding wheat:
Briefly, the above table shows that in 1956 the value per bushel of wheat marketed in Saskatchewan was almost 21 per cent below that of 1947. During the same period the western wheat grower's costs had risen by almost 46 per cent.

When you have a situation where farm costs have risen by 45 per cent over a period of 10 years, while farmers' returns for wheat have dropped by approximately 21 per cent, then I think you will agree with me that agriculture today is bound to be suffering as a consequence. It is not serving any good purpose to merely quote gross farm income because gross farm income by itself does not mean a thing. Therefore, we in this group will be very pleased to support the amendment to the amendment moved by the C.C.F.

On more than one occasion in the house the Minister of Agriculture has said he was not sure what it meant. He has suggested on various occasions that they have taken 1943-45 as the base period, and they set their support prices on those three years as the base. Your parity price would mean a different price if you took another base period. Parity to me means that a base period having been taken, a bushel of wheat or any other farm product would have the same purchasing power today as it had in that base period. That is as simple as it can be made, and it should be understandable to everyone in the house. In other words, the cost price relationship remains the same as it was in some previous base price period.
As far as the subamendment is concerned, I see nothing wrong with it, but I suggest there is a great deal of difference between the 100 per cent parity of income in the C.C.F. amendment and parity prices. Let us look at 100 per cent parity of income. Whose income is it going to be parity with? Whose income are you going to take?
