speechtext:
That is what this government has been doing for many years now. Apparently that is the policy of fee government as stated by the Minister of Finance.
We had a debate a few days ago regarding the price of eggs in this country. Egg prices are very low this year, from 22 to 23 cents a dozen to 30 cents a dozen for grade A large depending on the district where they are purchased. Yet in 1956, 68,321 cases of eggs were imported into this country. This was in the very year when prices went down to


the lowest level they had reached for years, away below the cost of production to the farmers.
Imports of dressed poultry last year totalled 22,816,809 pounds. That is the result of the policy of this government. I know that parts of this brief from the Canadian Horticultural Council were used this morning. I am not sure which parts were used, but I do want to say that fruit and vegetable growers all across this country are very disturbed about the importation of fruits and vegetables and the reduction in the prices received by our domestic producers. As was said by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) this morning, while these goods may not be dumped on the market in the strict legal sense of that word, they are nevertheless dumped as far as our domestic producers are concerned. Here is what the Canadian Horticultural Council considers to be the problem which its membership across Canada faces. This brief, which was sent to members of the cabinet, is dated February 4, 1957, and paragraph 3 reads:
It is doubtful if at any time in the past our primary producers of fruits and vegetables have been so exercised, or have suffered such serious losses as during the past few years, from the "dumping" of like products from the United States on the Canadian markets. These products may not be "dumped" within the limited definition of that term in the Customs Act or the Customs Tariff Act, but the effect on the financial returns of the Canadian farmer are just the same as though they had been "dumped" within the definition of the legislation.
The nature or form of the competition to which our producers object most strenuously is imports at "distress" prices at the peak or clean-up of United States harvesting which frequently collide with the commencement of Canadian harvesting. Under these conditions the United States producer may have received a premium price, or at least a good average price on a large proportion of his crop, but his "clean-up" sales can set the market price for a very large proportion of the Canadian crop of the same commodity, and prevent any possibility of the Canadian producer selling any portion of his crop at premium prices, or even benefiting to a normal extent from a short-crop condition that might exist in Canada.
As they point out, because fee United States lies south of us the crop season is earlier. There is very little importation into the United States of fruit and vegetables from other countries to the south, so they get a good price at the start of their season. But at the end of their season, which is probably the beginning of our season here, they dump their surplus in our market thus reducing the price which our own producers are able to get. I am sure the minister is aware of what the Canadian Horticultural Council has asked for in this connection. It

is set out in paragraph 6 of the brief under the heading "Our Request":
Our request to the government on behalf of these primary producers is as follows:
That the Minister of National Revenue be given power to establish a fair market value, effective during the Canadian marketing season, for each kind of fruit or vegetable of a kind produced in Canada, for the purpose of preventing "dumping" on Canadian markets.
I want to emphasize those words "produced in Canada". That is all they are asking. Naturally, they are not asking for a dumping duty on fruits and vegetables which are not produced here.
There is another point I wish to raise regarding the importation of agricultural products from the United States. I have here a cellophane pack in which turkeys are imported into this country from the United States. It should be plain what this brand name is. These bags are probably manufactured in the United States. The turkeys are packed in them over there and sent to this country-12 million pounds of them last year-though not all of them in these particular bags. Here we have United States turkeys sold under a Canadian brand name.
That, in my opinion, amounts to misrepresentation to the consumers of this country, and something should be done about it. It may be strictly within the law as far as the law reads at present, but in that case the law should be changed.
Not only turkeys are involved in this sort of practice; many other products are being treated in the same way. Incidentally, the brand name is Maple Leaf. Underneath the label it says the product was packed for this particular company whose head office is in Toronto, Canada. As I say, this is a situation which is being repeated with respect to a number of other products. I am told, though I do not know this as a fact, that United States potatoes are being shipped across the border from Maine into New Brunswick, packaged in Canadian bags and sold in competition with our own Ontario, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island potatoes; and that the shippers get the benefit of the maritime freight subsidy in competing against our own product. Is that right? I would ask the minister to make sure that it does not happen in the future.
Generally speaking, when people think of subsidies they seem to assume that farmers are the only people who receive them. That is not true. But it is generally accepted in the large centres of population that subsidies are linked with farmers, and that farmers have been given something for nothing. I would like to point out that in six of the
Agricultural Products-Support Prices last ten years, of the total subsidies paid by this government over 50 per cent went to non-agricultural industries. Only in four years did over 50 per cent go to agriculture, and those four years included the years when foot-and-mouth disease was raging in Canada. If it had not been for that, then probably for eight years out of ten over 50 per cent of the sums paid out in subsidies would have gone to non-agricultural industries. I am talking of direct subsidies, not of indirect subsidies of which I could name many.
We come now to the support prices act that the government has in operation. A year ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said on more than one occasion in the house 

in fact, he emphasized it-that it was absolutely necessary to have 78 million pounds of butter in the pipe line in order that the price could be maintained.

Mr. Speaker, as a number of speakers have said today, this is the third or fourth occasion during this session upon which we have discussed the question raised here, and most of those who have made that suggestion have also stated that they have delivered speeches before on the question. I am not in exactly the same position. I was not here when the first motion was moved on the 23rd of January and therefore did not take part in the discussion on that occasion. Again, there have been two occasions upon which the discussion was not quite in order and because I raised questions of order myself it was impossible for me to proceed with a discussion of the matter later.
Nevertheless the questions which have been discussed here have been discussed on many occasions both during this and other sessions and I think the opinion of most members is very well known. But apparently the question was raised today for a specific purpose, to

clarify some of the actions of at least some members of the house when the question was discussed before.
It was claimed by the last speaker, I think, that parity was first mentioned-I presume he meant in the house-by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) back in 1941. I am quite sure that the records will show that it was mentioned many times before that. But whether it was or was not, parity as we have been discussing it and as we understand it first became a matter of real discussion in the United States prior to 1932. After it had been discussed there for quite a number of years, they introduced their legislation which established their form of parity at that time. Some changes were made from time to time until by 1941 on the other side of the line they had considerable experience which we were able to follow. We had our discussions in the house in 1941. On that occasion I think it was quite apparent that the government at least had not been convinced by what had happened in the United States that we should adopt that policy here. But we were not required to make a decision on the matter until 1944. The chief reason why we were not required to make a decision was that we had with Britain throughout the war definite agreements under which we sold our farm products to Britain, not for the purpose of getting the highest possible returns from them-although we attempted to arrange a price which would be satisfactory to the farmers here-but for the purpose of getting a high production of our farm products in order to be able to supply food to the allied armies and to Great Britain. Hence during that period we did not consider that there was any real reason for adopting the marketing system based on parity prices. Nevertheless we kept close check on the matter.
However, in 1944, when the war was drawing toward a close, and when everyone knew it was drawing toward a close, we drafted the Agricultural Prices Support Act and had it passed by this parliament. The act did not actually come into effect or was not utilized until 1946 or 1947, I think, but it was placed on the statute books in 1944. The subsection about which there has been considerable discussion today is subsection 2 of section 9. Subsection 2 of section 9 states as follows:
(2) In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection one of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.

Agricultural Products-Support Prices
I should like to call attention to the fact, that until the last meeting of the provincial-dominion agricultural conference which was held in December last, the question which was discussed was not parity income. The question which was discussed was parity prices and no one left any doubt about that matter. We were discussing parity prices and usually were trying to have them brought in as they had been practiced in the United States. But during the last conference, after some discussion the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Mr. Hannam, made it apparent that they were not advocating parity prices but were advocating a parity of income; and from there on the discussions were associated with that term.
It was not their desire to say that there should be parity of prices. I think one of the reasons for that is apparent so far as the farmer is concerned. When you are dealing with parity prices you are dealing with the price of a commodity and it is possible to take the price of that commodity-whether it is butter, hogs or whatever it might be- and deal with that commodity by itself and prove that the farmer is not getting a parity price for that particular product when he sells it. But for all we know here or for all anyone knows who is discussing the question from that point of view, probably three-quarters of the farmers about whom he is talking do not produce that product at all. In other cases it can be said that the farmer may be getting a parity price on one particular commodity for the time being, may be getting less than parity on another, and he may be getting more than parity on still another and that he may be doing fairly well following the system he is following on his farm because he thinks a certain type of farming or a certain way of farming is the one best suited to the farm he is on and the district in which he is farming.
On the other hand, there are many farmers in our section of the country-that is out west, in Saskatchewan particularly-who grow only one commodity to sell, and that one commodity is wheat. Hence they are inclined to discuss the condition of the farmer altogether from the point of view of wheat growing. Of course that matter does not affect farmers in many other parts of the country. Hence to go on discussing questions from the point of view of whether eggs are at parity or whether some other commodity is at parity and whether you are helping someone in western Canada or someone in eastern Canada causes some persons to take to statistics-and probably I have been guilty of doing that myself-which apply right across Canada. But any time that
3326	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Support Prices I have used those statistics applying right across Canada I have called the attention of the hon. member who has just spoken and of every other hon. member of this house to the fact that no farmer who succeeds in farming ever bases the success or otherwise of his farming operations upon any one year, no matter where he is farming in Canada. Certainly he does not base it on any one year if he farms in western Canada and is a wheat grower because you can grow wheat of the kind that we grow only in a country that is comparatively dry; and any country that is comparatively dry has drought years in which the farmers cannot grow wheat at all or anything else, scarcely. Hence to start figuring from that point of view, either by giving the figures right across the country or by applying them to any one year, does not help very much in considering what is the position of the farmer.
I therefore repeat that I have never relied upon any comparisons with the year 1951. The year 1951 is a top year in income returns to farmers right across this country. It is a top year because we were fighting a war in Korea. Everyone knows that just a short while prior to that time all farmers were quite convinced that the prices of the things they were going to buy were going down because there was less and less use for steel, aluminum and all of the commodities that enter in the production of farm implements. We had just got out of a war. Just when we were on the point of thinking that the change was going to come about, we were into another war.
As soon as we got into the other war, farmers were competing with those who were conducting the war in the buying of their equipment. Of course, prices went up. They could not go in any other direction. Since that time we have had other experiences, one of which we are in the midst of now having to do with Suez, and which still causes people to think that we are approaching a period when there may be use for equipment of a kind that cannot be used on the farms.
As a matter of fact, the old story has never changed. At one period you are beating plowshares into swords and at another period you are beating swords into plowshares. When we are compelled to buy in competition with those who are beating plowshares into swords, our prices are high. If anyone tells the young people of this country that they are foolish to stay on the farms because we are going through an experience of that kind, well, to say the least he is not speaking in the interests of the


country itself, nor is he giving the kind of incentive or direction to the young people which should be given.
My main criticism of the propaganda that has been put out in this country for the last four or five years is that if any young man or young woman listened to it none of them would go near a farm. If any young man or young woman who was already on a farm was told that everyone who works in some other industry is getting far more than they are, then they would not remain on the farm. My friends over in the C.C.F. group have forgotten that they used to say that all these industries they are talking about were in the hands of 50 big shots. Probably they were a lot closer to the truth then than they are now. The young people who go away from the farms do not step into the shoes of the 50 big shots. It is only those people who get elected and become ministers in a C.C.F. government who get into the $10,000 a year category. This is just a matter of having one point of view when you are in one class and an entirely different point of view when you are in another; it is quite understandable.
But I do submit that it is not a good thing to be going around the country telling the young people stories like that. What are the results? During the time we were in the conference last December the farmers' union brought in representatives of those who worked in the implements industry in this country and made representations that something ought to be done for the farmers in order to make it possible for them to buy more farm implements so the young people who had been employed in the implement industry could get back into it. When they submitted their figures they showed that a short time ago there were 15,000 young men and women working in the farm implement industry in this country; last December, when they were talking to us, there were less than 5,000.
At the time I asked where they got the extra 10,000 who came into the industry after the war. They told me they got them off the farms. I said, where did they go when 10,000 of them could not find jobs any longer with you? They said, we do not know. Of course, they did not know. I said, what did they do about the houses they had bought in the cities where they went? We do not know. You and I know that they bought houses in the places to which they went on the basis of prices that existed, and which were three or four times as high as they were not very many years ago. These people were asked to pay for them on what was approximately a rental basis, paying so much a month or a year. It would have taken many of them 10

or 30 years to pay for them if they had remained in them. When they lost their jobs, where did they go? I do not know. I only know what I did myself when I was young, and what many others did when we were misled into thinking that it was a good thing to get off the farm. We often lost what we put into homes.
If this kind of talk goes on during a period when it is obvious that the cost of materials which we are going to use must be high, and during a time when many of the experts are saying it is not always going to continue that way when our experience has taught us it never has continued that way for the greater part of a period, then I do not think it is helping this country at all. Some people say to not go near a farm; you cannot make any money there. They say you cannot get yourself established because there is no way by which you can borrow money in order to get a farm. Statements of this sort are not going to help the country. They will lead to the young people getting away from the farm and staying as far away as they can. Eventually, if we can judge by the experience of the past, many of them are going to wish they could get back again. So far as I am concerned, I am not making those kind of speeches. I like to be accused of not making them, because I believe they are not in the interests of the country or in the interests of the young people either.
We have had considerable talk about parity prices and what this means, as well as the statement made by Mr. King. This point has been answered over and over again, but probably it should be answered again. Mr. King had a picture of what the farmer had gone through before the war, and many of us had, too. This morning the Leader of the Opposition repeated something that has been said in this house by C.C.F. members on a number of occasions. I am not too sure whether or not he meant exactly what he said. Probably he did not mean as much as I am taking out of it because of the fact others have stated it before. He was comparing the value of a dollar made today with the value of a dollar in those days before the war. He went on to suggest, if he did not say it definitely, and I think he said it definitely, that conditions are as bad now as they were then.

The net position involves many things that my hon. friend has not put into the statement he has made, which he says means the same thing. It does not mean the same thing. A farmer is thinking, not only in terms of dollars and cents for the year 1956 but in terms of a lifetime and an activity in which he is bringing up a family. To try to tell him that the only thing he must take into consideration when he is going to decide whether he is to stay on the farm or get away from it is the net return for a particular year, or a particular month, or a particular week, will not profit you much. I repeat, if you wish to go into a discussion of the question with the farmers on that basis you will not get very far. The farmer, in some areas, in making his comparisons looks at the neighbourhood in which he lives and he says that in 1931 to 1937 my children were running around barefooted in the middle of the winter and I had to keep them under

Agricultural Products-Support Prices cover; I could not buy shoes for them. If you want to try to convince him that that condition exists now, hop to it. I will not need to answer you on it because the condition is not the same and everybody knows it is not the same.
If we are concerned about keeping young people on the farm I think we ought to be a little more careful about what we say and how we say it and how we put it, and I am concerned with that and I am sure that other members of the house are as well.
To come back to the relationship between the position we were in and the position we are in now, that is the position we were in in 1944 when this act was drafted, may I say we were in the middle of what we then thought would be the last three years of the war, 1943, 1944 and 1945. Everyone who wrote to us at that time was asking, and everyone at any meetings where we went was suggesting, that if we could just keep the times and the conditions to where they were then we would feel satisfied about it. The thing which was in their minds was what happened at the end of the first world war, when those of us who went on the farms around that time were expecting a continuation for some little time of the conditions that had prevailed just at the end of the war and had prevailed a year or two before. But we found out that we were very greatly mistaken, and that after wars governments in the past had not paid very much attention to the condition of the farmer. As a matter of fact, they had used the farmer to beat down this thing they called inflation. On every occasion that anyone in this house can remember following a war that was done. Economist after economist, in writing about the wars of the past, has intimated that that was done, and a certain school of economists argued that the only position to take to prevent inflation and to put things back to where they had been was to beat down the prices of primary commodities and more particularly farm prices, and that was done.
What Mr. King had in his mind and what every member of the government had in his mind was that that should not happen after the last war; that it had happened after the first one but that it should not happen after the last one. I am not discussing anything political when I say that because the Liberals came to power not long after the first war, and some of these things did happen and kept on happening. I am simply saying that that is a fact of history, recorded in every history book that has ever been written and recorded in the writings of every economist who has ever written; that at the ends of wars the only way you can get back is to grind down the primary producers and make

it possible for people to get back into employment or into industry of some kind or another.
The intention when this legislation was drafted was to see that that did not happen.
I am sure that whatever other criticisms hon. members can make at this time they will agree that that has not happened up until now. I am not going to say that this government is responsible for all of that. We have simply been attempting to do in our own way what has been attempted elsewhere. Britain has been bent on seeing that it did not happen after the last war; the United States has been bent on seeing that it did not happen after the last war. We have been working along with them, and others in their own way have been working in the same direction in other countries throughout the world. I think it is only fair to say that wherever you go the same things have not happened since the last war that happened after the one preceding it, and we are benefiting greatly from the actions which have been taken.
Among other things we took this action. Some people who are more conservative than we are, and maybe some people in our own party who are more conservative than I am, seem to think that we should not have any of those controls; we should not have any price controls; we should not start to try to move people around; we should let them act entirely upon their own. We did not agree with that and therefore we brought in this legislation to make it possible for something else to be done.
Under the legislation a revolving fund of $200 million has been set up. The general statement that is made when people want to be critical of the legislation is that we have only used, for a while they said $10 million, now I think they admit that probably $90 million has been used. But the fact is that upwards of $400 million has been used. After having bought up 75 million pounds of butter, as was suggested here a few moments ago, and put it in storage, we sold the 75 million pounds of butter and got the money back and put it back into the fund. That is what is meant by a revolving fund. Between $350 million and $400 million-I have not the exact figure-was used for that purpose. It is a fact that we have been able to replenish the fund from time to time. That has made it possible to carry on this legislation continuously since 1944 down to the present time. Anyone who is critical of the legislation, those people who think in terms of stopping inflation by some of these other methods, are not arguing against the $200 million being there now, because it has never been necessary to go back to the treasury to get another cent over the $200 million. We have been utilizing

the fund that is there, putting up the money that is necessary to put up for the time being, selling the commodities after a while and getting the money back and putting it into the fund.
Somebody asks, why do you need to do that; why do you not set the price? I have repeated this over and over in the house. We have no authority to set the price. The only time we ever had the authority to set the price was when the War Measures Act was in operation, and it came into operation right after the war started and continued in effect for about four years after the war. During that time we could set the prices; we could say what the price of potatoes was; we could say what the price of butter was; we could say what the price of anything was; we could tell you what wages you had to work for, and so on. But immediately the War Measures Act went out of operation we had no such authority; but every authority that is possible exists somewhere in this country with some government, and that authority rests with the provincial governments. That is why we have the marketing act before the house at the present time, in order to pass some of the authority which we have over to the provinces so that they can enforce some of the things that they are doing. But the provincial government has that authority and no one else. If grade A eggs sold in the province of Ontario at 21 cents and 22 cents there never was any reason for their selling at that price.
This government said, "You can put them into a storage at a price of 38 cents". The only cost involved was that of getting them from where they were produced to the storage by some organization-a private organization or a co-operative organization, whatever was desired to be set up in order to get these eggs to the storage plant-and they were turned over to us on the basis of 38 cents. The only authority that could say that had to be done was the provincial authority and there is not a provincial government in Canada that has done it. Therefore I say if we have not had full benefit of the supports that have been put there then it is not the fault of the federal government. That is our way of getting around the constitution.

To begin with, when the bill incorporating this company was first placed before parliament there was a clear-cut undertaking that the line would be an all-Canadian line. Not one of them is an insurance company; not one of them is an investment company. They are all in the oil or pipe-line business.
That is hardly playing fair with a committee of this house or with parliament. When this matter was last before us I was at the point of drawing attention to the strange phenomenon that the two main officials of the company who appeared before our committee had not compared notes as to the information which was in their possession. The president of the company, Mr. Morrison, was asked about the share holdings of the directors of the company, and he said on page 54:
I know how many a certain number of companies have. But I have no knowledge whatever of how many individual directors may have.
However, on the very next page, under questioning by my colleague the hon. member for Mackenzie, Mr. McQuarrie said:
Part of my duty is to check each year to see if each director is properly qualified. According to the list which I had on April 5, 1956, at that time one director owned two shares; another owned 5,000; one owned 202; another, 102; another 302; two owned some 2,000, and another one owned five.
Mr. Morrison, however did not know how many shares the directors held; indeed he said:
That is the first time I ever heard this.
It seems strange indeed that these two principal spokesmen of the company appearing before our committee had not compared notes as to the information they had concerning their own company.
I draw attention also to the fact that this company has stated repeatedly-in its explanatory note to the bill, through those who spoke for it in the Senate, through the hon. gentleman who is sponsoring the bill in this house and through those who appeared in the committee-that its purpose is to secure a wider distribution of the shares of the company among the general public. Yet on page 44 of the minutes of proceedings

In addition to these instances of lack of fairness with parliament there is another matter which we feel is particularly serious, and I say quite frankly that we have this additional information only because we have delayed the passing of this bill, only because with the passage of time certain information which had not reached the light of day when the company was before the standing committee on March 7 has now come to light. I ask the sponsor of the bill to read again the minutes of proceedings and evidence, as he must have done many times during the past few weeks. He will note that the witnesses, the president and the secretary, were very careful to make sure that the information they gave to the committee was dated not later than April 5, 1956. For example, I draw attention to page 55 where Mr. McQuarrie had been asked certain questions. On two occasions he indicated that he was talking about "The list I had on April 5, 1956". It is very interesting to note that when Mr. McQuarrie was pressed by the hon. member for Bow River regarding certain stock holdings he replied:
The stock register is about three inches thick. I did not bring it along. It has about 6,000 names in it.
Is a book three inches thick too heavy to carry? I have one here two or three inches thick that I brought in from the library. If one is interested in a matter and wants to tell the whole story, why not bring it along? As I indicated the other day, it is also rather interesting that the notice to the shareholders concerning the meeting at which the question of this stock split was discussed was not brought along. That is noted on page 63 where Mr. McQuarrie says:
I wish we had brought the notice. A letter went out to each shareholder, along with the notice. I have not got a copy of that letter with me.
My point is that if the committee had had the notice and the letter calling that special meeting, the committee would then have learned of any other items that were discussed at that special meeting, and if the witnesses had brought to the committee the stock register hon. members would have been in a position to ask questions with respect to

whether there were any more shares out since the date of April 5, 1956, which was the date the witnesses gave as the deadline beyond which they were giving no information.
The fact is that an annual meeting of this company was held on April 18, 1956, in the city of Vancouver but nothing that trans-spired at that annual meeting on April 18, 1956, came out at the meeting that was held in this building on March 7, 1957. Surely it was relevant to the affairs of this company to bring before this committee any important decisions that had been taken at the annual meeting on April 18, 1956. I now tell this committee that at that meeting on April 18, 1956, the shareholders approved of the issue of several thousand options to purchase shares. The decision to issue these options had been made by the board of directors in October, 1955, and according to the Financial Post "Survey of Industrials" for 1956-and it is also indicated in Moody's "Transportation Manual" for 1956-4,900 of the options that were approved at the annual meeting in April, about which we were told nothing in the committee, were issued to persons who turned them into shares at a price of $38,625. These sales were made in 1956.
The price on the market of Trans Mountain shares during 1956 varied, of course, but in January it was $46, in February $47, and in March it was running around $51. In other words, the people who got these options, which were decided upon by the board of directors in October, 1955, and approved by the annual meeting in April, 1956, got shares in this company at a price which at the time they bought them was less than the market price.
After the annual meeting in April, 1956, at which time approval was given to the 4,900 shares which had been sold between October, 1955, and April, 1956, approval was given to still further options. May I make the point here, that all of these options were to certain key employees and not to the general public.
My hon. friend comes before the house and says that the aim of the company is to bring about a wider distribution to the Canadian public. We have been told about the
1,500,000	shares issued out of the treasury, but deep, dark secrecy was maintained with regard to these options that were made available to key employees, to personnel and management, on the basis of which a handsome profit has been made as the result of the stock splitting technique.
I happen to have on my desk a very interesting article from the New York Times of March 24, 1957. The title is "Prices Anticipate Splits of Shares". It is an analysis of what happens to stocks when companies decide on

stock splits. It points out that the time when the value of shares appreciates really commences when the rumour first gets out that a stock split is going to take place, and the time when the appreciation takes place and values accrue runs from the time the rumour leaks out that it is going to take place through the time when the directors decide on it, through the time when the shareholders decide on it and up until the time when the split is actually approved. The article is based on the experience in some 28 different stocks that were analysed by Mr. Burton Crane, a writer in the New York Times.
I submit that what this company was doing in this whole piece was to go in for the stock-splitting technique by letting rumours out that it was going to happen and by sending out notices to the shareholders so the rumour would spread still more, and the result was that the market price of these shares went up and up. That was fine for those who held stock but it was a particular bonanza for those on the inside who were being given these options about which not a word was said before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines when these people came before the committee on March 7 of this year.
I would point out that one of the reasons we are now in possession of this information is that we have exercised our right to debate this matter and have exercised our right, if you will, to delay it. In the meantime there has come to light the annual report of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. It is for the period ended December 31, 1956, and I am sure that whatever is in the material contained in the annual report for the calendar year 1956 must have been in the possession of these gentlemen who were before our committee on March 7, 1957, but of course no reference was made to it.
However that annual report has now been published. It bears the date of April 4, 1957, but is for the period ended December 31, 1956. I have not yet been able to obtain a copy of it. I am informed that it is not yet available in Ottawa but it is available in Toronto. By long distance telephone only today I have been able to get some of the information contained in that annual report. I dare say my hon. friend who is sponsoring this bill may have a copy of it. I hope he has, and if he has I hope he will agree that the information contained in that annual report should be given to the house even though it was not given to the committee when it met on March 7, 1957.
I urge again that hon. members read the evidence taken before that committee, as I have read it two or three times. When you 82715-211

read it, after you get hold of this information that there were these options and these additional shares, you then begin to realize how cleverly these witnesses avoided getting into that field by giving the committee information on the question of shares only up to April 5, 1956. I repeat that it was in March, 1957, that these gentlemen were here, but the latest information given to the committee was information up to April 5, 1956. As I say, if they had had the stock register with them these other questions would have arisen and it might have been possible for members to get this information.
The shares that are being optioned out to key employees at the present time, and that includes any directors who are also employees of the company and on salary, have been granted at $82 per share. At the present time they are selling on the market for something of the order $115 to $120. So there again you have a special profit being made available to these key employees, including any salaried personnel engaged in the management of the company.
I must say this to hon. gentlemen around who know the practice in these companies. I recognize that this is standard practice, this business of splitting shares and this business of granting options to employees and to management personnel at a price less than the market price. But when a company is coming before parliament and asking parliament to bless a manoeuvre of this kind I suggest that it is the moral responsibility of that company to let parliament know what is happening. Oh, they did not make any misstatements with regard to this matter. They carefully avoided getting anywhere near it; they carefully avoided the question of shares that had been issued since April 5, 1956, and they carefully avoided getting anywhere near the question of any decision about shares that had been made at the annual meeting of April 18, 1956. Indeed, they carefully avoided even mentioning the annual meeting that was held in Vancouver on April 18, 1956.
I say in passing that we have had in this House of Commons one other case of options about which we had no information, options which were just pieces of paper in the hands of two gentlemen in particular and which, as a result of the action of parliament-against which some of us fought for all we were worth-became extremely valuable. Now we have these people-key personnel or key employees, to use the language of the report that is out, a copy of which we have not yet been able to get-being given options to buy at a price less than the market price. Why is the market price soaring? It is not

Private Bills
just because the company is making high profits, although that is a factor in the picture as well and in that connection there are elements that one must bear in mind. It is also because this company has indulged in this stock-splitting technique, starting with the rumour, then the notice, the special meeting and so on which, as Burton Crane of the New York Times says, has turned out to be a standard way of appreciating the stocks of a company such as this one.
Incidentally, before I touch upon the point I was going to make, may I point out that at page 44, under questioning, the witness- it was Mr. Morrison in both cases-said at two places: "The company is not selling any more shares." That is to be found about a third of the way down the page and then further down again he says "not that additional shares will be issued". I leave it to Mr. Morrison to justify that statement that no more shares were being sold in the light of the fact that these options bad been issued to sell additional shares out of the treasury, out of the 3j million shares that were not issued in the first instance.
To recapitulate the story of this company, may I say that in the first instance 1,500,000 shares were issued and we have been given the breakdown as to those shares as between companies and private individuals. Later on 4,900 shares were issued between October 1955 and April 1956 on the basis of options agreed to in October, 1955. That seemed to bring the total number of shares issued to 1,504,900. When the witness gave the figure, he gave it as 1,504,928 as at April 5, 1956. I cannot seem to account for the other 28 shares but we will not argue about that matter. My point is that since that date, when that was the figure, more thousands of shares have been issued. They had been issued after the date of April 5, 1956, and before the witnesses appeared before the committee. They had been issued out of the treasury and yet the committee was not told about that fact. They said they were not selling any more shares. But they were selling shares to key personnel and they were doing so at a price below the market price, thus enabling them to make a special profit from the gains arising because of the stock-splitting transaction.
The company has said a number of times that it has no thought of making any profit out of this deal. For example, at page 45 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee, I find Mr. Morrison reported as saying this:
The question of profit in this transaction has never come up on the board.

At page 46 we find that Mr. Morrison was asked this question by and made this answer to the hon. member for Nanaimo:
Q. Well, is there any value whatsoever to the company and to the present shareholders to be obtained from this measure? A. Not that I know of.
Also over on page 48 we find that Mr. Morrison, in answer to the hon. member for Nanaimo, stated this:
There is no thought of making a profit out of it.
When they made those statements these people knew that these options were out. If either of these witnesses is himself a salaried employee of the company he certainly was entitled to these options and probably had them, and was therefore a person who would be making a profit out of this whole stocksplitting manoeuvre.
In order to establish their honesty these men may say, "Oh, but that profit was already made because of the rumour that there would be a stock split, because of the decision of the board of directors, because of the decision of the shareholders, because of the appreciation that had already taken place". They may say that there will be no further profit to them as a result of parliament passing the bill, if it does pass. If they want to take that position, the only answer I make is that what they are doing is asking parliament to bless a transaction the aim of which was to make profit for those on the inside and that, in the light of that fact, these people have not been fair with parliament. That is why we say that this bill should not be passed by this House of Commons.
We make no apology for the delay with which this bill has been met as a result of our close study and our close scrutiny of it. In fact, we think we have done a service to parliament in holding this bill up until we could get all this information which was kept secret, which was carefully avoided by the company's spokesmen, so that we might know the whole story. We say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the committee that in the light of the evidence to which I have referred we do not accept the statement that the only purpose of this legislation is to achieve a wider distribution of the shares amongst the general public. We say that the purpose of this legislation is to ask parliament to bless a stock-splitting manoeuvre which is of advantage to those on the inside, and that is why we are opposed to this bill.

The company proposes an expansion program. Why does it propose this? It does so

because Alberta has between 200,000 and
300,000	barrels of oil a day which it wishes to export, and they want to pass it over the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line to Vancouver.
Some of it is going to go to the United States, but what is wrong with that? We sell lumber, fish and all kinds of things to the United States. We are complaining, on the one hand, that we have this adverse balance of trade with the United States. This will help to correct it.
By the way, in the Vancouver Sun of last Thursday, April 4, I found an article indicating that the British American Oil Company proposes to build a new refinery at Port Moody in the constituency of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. It is going to cost about $20 million and it is going to be supplied with oil by the Trans Mountain Pipe Line from Alberta and so help to build up industries in the Vancouver area. This plant will have a capacity of about 20,000 barrels a day and will give employment to about 175 people.
Why does the company wish to propose that its stock be split? Most companies do this when the price of their shares on the stock market rises to such a price that they get out of reach of the ordinary investor. It is considered unwise and perhaps detrimental to the interests of a company to have shares selling at too high a price as they would then tend to gravitate into the hands of a few rich people. The company is subjected to criticism, so it is considered wise to split the stock so that a great number of shares will be available for ordinary trading by people of modest means. It means that there are a great number of people interested in the welfare of the company and able to support it.
A good deal has been said by my friends opposite as to why the company does not sell some treasury stock. There are about 3.5 million shares of treasury stock and they ask why the company does not sell it. In the first place, there are several ways in which a company may finance its expansion program. I am hurrying because I promised to be through in 15 or 20 minutes and I want to give other members an opportunity to vote. Let me say that this company proposes in the coming year to expend $40 million, and over the next two years about $70 million. The company has started construction of two loops, one near Edson and one just north of Kamloops, for the purpose of increasing the capacity of the line so that they can bring the oil from Alberta to the Pacific coast and so as to help Alberta to pay greater dividends. It is a prosperous company. There is no question about that.
[Mr. Fairey.l
It is true that they lost money for the first two years, and they have made money in the succeeding years. They are plowing all the money back into capital expenditures.
The $70 million the company proposes to spend in the next two years is to be raised by a $30 million bond issue. Why do they not sell shares as my friends opposite request? In the first place, they do not wish to finance in that way because at the present time the bond market is the best means of financing. Financial people, like Wood, Gundy and Company, and others, suggest that at the present time the most economical way of financing capital expenditure is by bond issues, and therefore it is not necessary to sell the shares. This may not be true in every year from now on when the tremendous growth in British Columbia and Alberta is realized. It is evidently expected that this pipe line will have to be enlarged or a duplicate line built. At that time it may be very handy to have a sufficient number of shares in the treasury so that they could be marketed if the market conditions meant the company should resort to that type of financing.
There is no point in trying to blacken the name of a company which is operating successfully, which is doing a good job and which is carrying oil for export as well as for the full requirements, I may say, of British Columbia, and where there has not been a single share sold except for cash with the exception of those of which I spoke a few moments ago. These are available on option to fulltime employees after they have been employed one year after applying for the option.
There are many things I might say but I am going to close with this. In his closing speech the other night the hon. member for Nanaimo-I excuse him for this because I know he had to jump up quickly to talk the bill out and therefore he was probably not as accurate as one would normally expect him to be-

I certainly am not. The second inaccurate statement which he made had to do with the shares. There is no secret about it, the main shareholders of this company are big oil companies, and they are not selling their shares on the stock market. Richfield has 50,000, Union Oil of California, 100,000; making in all 670,000 shares.

These people hold these shares because they wish to hold control and management of the company because it is their oil which is passing over the line. Then, 250,000 shares were sold to the Western Canadian Oil Company.
The hon. gentleman said the other day that when they were asking for the names of the shareholders they were misled by a statement of Mr. McQuarrie that the shares were held by a variety of people, including companies and other people and, as it says in the evidence, people who had money to invest. I promised to sit down after I talked for 15 or 20 minutes. I have spoken for nearly 20 minutes. There is much more I could say. Let me say this in closing. There is nothing underhand about this thing. This is a normal procedure for companies. When shares of a company reach too high a price on the market they split the shares to make them more readily available to those of us who are in the lower income brackets so that we may have a chance to participate in the profits of a good company. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we
adjourned at six o'clock I was pointing out that governments throughout the world had been endeavouring to prevent conditions after the last war resembling those which had followed most wars in the past, namely conditions which resulted from an effort to curb inflation by forcing down the prices of primary products, and that Canada, in trying to avoid that situation, had introduced the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944 under which we had utilized $200 million as a revolving fund for the purpose of supporting prices.
I indicated that we had no authority to set prices. We therefore undertook to buy any products which others would not buy, at a certain set price. We had dealt with hogs, we had dealt with butter and I was about to deal a little more fully with eggs. My occasion for wishing to deal a little more
[The Deputy Chairman.]
fully with eggs and certain other commodities is provided by the annual presentation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and members of the cabinet on February 15, 1957. I should like to review shortly some of the things which were said before six o'clock in order to link them with the suggestions made by the federation of agriculture.
The first commodity dealt with by the federation as a separate commodity was dairy products, but before coming to that they dealt with the general question of supports. Part of that representation was read by the Leader of the Opposition. I would like to read another part of it:
We therefore suggest that a greater use be made in the future of the Agricultural Prices Support Act as a means of maintaining adequate market support prices of those farm commodities to which the act applies. Eggs, fowl and turkeys provide immediate opportunities for the application of this request.
In so far as eggs are concerned, the decision of the federation taken at Winnipeg and later presented to the government was to the effect that we had not been able to maintain the price which we had sought to maintain by saying we would take delivery at 38 cents of all eggs which were delivered to storage at given times. During the early part of our experience, beginning about six years ago, we set the 1st day of December as the day on which those eggs might be delivered, and we found as we went along that it is much more difficult to deal effectively with eggs than it is to deal with butter, the chief reason being that butter production is governed largely by weather conditions; in Canada we have a very high production in the summer months and a very low production in the winter months, due to the fact that our cows are out to grass in the summer and are fed on dry feed in the winter time. We have attempted to overcome the disadvantages of this situation, as I stated before dinner, by stabilizing the price throughout the year.
When we begin to deal with eggs it is quite different. There was a time when the period at which egg production was high was regulated by the fact that the old hen started to cluck in the spring of the year; eggs were put under her and she finally hatched them out. That always happened about the same time of the year, so we thought we were in a position to carry on in the usual way over a period of time.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: Too many cluckers in the government.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
The hatcheries have changed all that. Individuals who are quite anxious to cluck in here find means of operating

hatcheries so as to produce eggs whenever they want them, not when the hen decides to have them. So the hatchers decided-or somebody decided and the hatchers followed along-that around December 1 would be a good time to have a lot of eggs, because the government was prepared to take delivery of them if they were sent to storage; and now we have a very high production of eggs around December and January. This has been giving us some trouble, and it is that trouble to which the federation is referring, and to which it was referring when it discussed this question in Winnipeg.
And having listened to these discussions, and having heard the representations, we did, within a few days, follow the suggestions which the federation made. This document is dated February 15, so as a matter of fact we had already started before it was delivered. On January 24, I think it was, we offered to take delivery of grade A large eggs at 38 cents; not to wait until December 1 but to purchase them and put them in storage, if no one else would put them in storage. So we purchased grade A large eggs at 38 cents and if they were oil-dipped we paid 39 cents for them-it costs about one cent to dip them. If we paid 38 cents we oil-dipped them before putting them in storage.
This was of some assistance, as the federation said in its representations to the government. But another problem has developed in connection with eggs which at that time was not even recognized. In this presentation to the government it has been suggested that we should establish a proper relationship between the price of grade A large eggs and medium eggs. The reason for that was that there had been a "spread", as high almost as 20 cents I think at times in the immediate past, between the price of grade A large eggs and medium eggs.
According to the best experts from whom we could get advice, the real relationship in weight between the medium egg and the grade A large egg is about five cents. So the suggestion was that we should set some margin between the two by establishing a price for both grade A large eggs and medium eggs.
Unfortunately for those who held that view the spread between grade A large eggs and medium eggs has been from one to two cents for weeks now, and of course there had to be a reason for that. Some people seem to think that supply and demand have nothing to do with these things, but it is found now that because pullets are not laying at this particular time, again because of the time that the hatcheries bring them to life, medium eggs are low in volume

At the same time it has been found that because there has been some difficulty about selling old hens due to the price not having been as high for a while, the old hen population has increased with the result that the supply of grade A large eggs has also increased and there are more grade A large eggs on the market than the market will take and not quite as many medium eggs on the market as the market will take. Therefore there is only a spread of one or two cents between the prices of the two.
It is all very well for people to say after a thing happens: "Well, you should have foreseen all that." I might suggest that if I had been running a hatchery I probably would have foreseen some of it. But we have not been doing that so we have had to find some method of dealing with the matter. Our method was, first, to purchase grade A large eggs and, second, to keep a very close check on the medium eggs, and we did not see that increasing the support price over and above what it is now would correct that situation very much if at all.
But it is found that there are eggs coming on the market that do not come under these grades at all. They are what we call grade B eggs. There may be a few misshaped eggs among them. There may be some that are not quite as clean as they should be. There may be a few that have been cracked, and there are other things that happen to them. The result is that they are not fit for storage. But those eggs can be utilized here and there across the country and take the place of well graded and well fed eggs with the result that those who carry on the producing of eggs in the manner in which they should suffer so far as price is concerned.
Therefore we have decided to put a support price under B eggs, take those eggs off the market immediately, freeze them and sell them for baking purposes. That plan has just been inaugurated and put into effect. We think it will work in order to bring about the results that are desired. I have recited the plan here to make it known in the first place that we are working in that direction and to indicate in the second place that when representations of this kind are made to us by those who should know we do take action upon them as soon as possible.
Another matter was brought to our attention at that time having to do with other commodities. The one I am most concerned about at the moment is dairy products. As I stated before dinner, we have had a support price on butter for the last six or seven years. The reason why we placed a support price under butter was that for many years
3342	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Support Prices before the war we had been depending upon cheese taking the surplus milk, milk that was not required as whole milk for human consumption, milk that was not required for the purpose of producing butter. We had been putting that into cheese. It was the lowest price milk that went on the market and the cheese industry was carried on in a rather big way for the purpose of supplying the British market. We had a market even during the war for 145 million pounds of cheese in Great Britain.
But when the war was over the British did not seem to desire to have our cheese at the price that we thought we must secure for it and that market has fairly well disappeared, first, because we are not producing the cheese to send to it and, second, because if we were going to produce it we had to have a much higher price than could be obtained if the production of cheese was to be used to take up the surplus supply of milk. When we ceased to put our surplus milk in cheese we desired to put more of it into butter. We therefore established a support price to keep up production.
In the meantime, partly because of the fact that we had been at war, a great deal more milk was being put into cans and a great deal more was being turned into skim milk powder. A rather recent development so far as quantity is concerned had to do with the development of powdered skim milk, and two different processes were used in its preparation. The document presented to the government by the federation suggested that we should place a support price of 14 cents under roller skim powder and 16 cents under spray skim powder. We considered the matters, examined the whole situation as it exists and decided to place a support price under both these commodities.
Two or three weeks ago I announced to the house that we had put a support price of 14 cents on roller powder and 17 cents on spray. As was suggested by one member of the opposition this afternoon, the figure of 17 cents is one cent more than we were asked for, and we had a reason for doing that. Since the representations were made we had been watching carefully the price of skim milk powder and had found it had been running around 16, 16J, 17, 17J and even as high as 18 cents. Again, the price which farmers in Canada were receiving for milk going into the product was not as high as the price in the United States, and we made some inquiries as to why that was the condition and came to certain conclusions.
Something was said this afternoon to the effect that we had not had any support price under powdered milk prior to a few


weeks ago, but that is not the case. We had had a support under skim milk powder for several years, and that support was in this form. We said to the producers of the powder: "Whenever you have a surplus that you are not able to handle or market the government will consider taking that surplus and holding it off the market or giving it away to someone who is in need of it", usually in some other part of the world, "and you can rest assured that we will do that from time to time."
Looking back I know that I can say, and it can be said by others, that that would not be a very satisfactory manner to deal with the situation from the point of view of the producer because too much risk was left with the person who was accumulating the surplus, and so we decided to guarantee that we would take the powder at 14 cents for the one variety and 17 cents for the other, with the result that the price of milk going into those commodities immediately rose from 5 to 10 cents a hundred, and even milk going into the production of butter has increased in price. I think that is only natural because of the fact that those who are dealing in this commodity now know that they can turn it over to the government at a price if they should have a surplus and therefore they can go out and pay the farmer a higher price for his milk.
It is encouraging to note that the element of competition in purchasing entered into it to such an extent that, generally speaking, the price has gone up five cents to ten cents and there are indications of its having gone up about 15 cents in some places. Hence that has had a beneficial result to the dairy farmer right across Canada. Those are two of the things that have been done as a result of the representation made by the federation at that time. Then they go on to say:
Based on the Supreme Court of Canada decision respecting the Ontario farm products marketing act it is clear that further federal legislation is needed if producer boards are to be enabled to carry on certain functions which they consider will often be essential to effective orderly marketing of farm products.
That bill is before the house. I had the privilege of speaking to it yesterday. I was a little bit surprised when the Leader of the Opposition took the position in relation to it that we should not place the onus of proof on the person who was accused of marketing a product outside the provincial act or that the onus of proof should not be placed upon the individual who was charged.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
I questioned it. I have
now looked into the matter and I may say that any criticism on my part in that regard was not well founded.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
I am pleased to know that my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition sometimes comes to conclusions that an opinion he had earlier is not right. I am sure there will not be the same emphasis put upon any difficulties some of the rest of us have in seeing as far into the future as some people think we should. But on this occasion the representations were made from Ontario that we should pass legislation and the main part of that legislation is the fact that the onus of proof had to be placed upon the person who was being charged to prove that the product was a product that was either being marketed within the province in which it was produced or was one that was being marketed to be sold outside the province in which it was produced. That legislation is before the house and carries out another of the requests which were made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at that time.
There is still one other matter, namely tariff policy. The federation of agriculture said this:
In the case of potatoes, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture repeats its request that a year round duty of 37i cents per hundredweight be applied to commercial and seed potato importations into Canada from the United States.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) reported to the house two days ago that that has been done. I just review these few things in order to indicate that when representations are made by the farm movement we look into those matters and have them dealt with. This afternoon there was some suggestion that there are special reasons at the moment for dealing with them. May I say that the main reason for dealing with them at this time is that they were asked for in the last representation which was made to this government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. If that happens to come at a time when it is a little bit inconvenient for the opposition, of course we are not making any excuse for having made the changes at this time. The fact is that we have been dealing with these commodities and have been paying attention to the representations that have been made from time to time by the farmers. I think that is sufficient to indicate that we pay some attention to the representations that are made to us.
That brings me to the point of saying that after all the most important consideration in connection with all this discussion is where we have arrived by carrying on the policies which we have carried on. I am not, of course, discussing the grain position. That matter does not come under this department nor does it come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. The other products come
9,	1957	3343
Agricultural Products-Support Prices under it, and any farm products that are not mentioned in the act up to now other than grain can come under that act.
I have here before me a list of the prices that have been obtained on the Canadian side of the line for these products recently and I have them over a longer period of time. However, in order to save time I think I will deal with the most recent prices which we have been able to secure. On April 5, 1957 good slaughter steers sold at Toronto for $20 a hundredweight and in Chicago at $19.50.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: That does not mean anything.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: My hon. friend says that does not mean anything. It means $20, which is 50 cents a hundredweight higher than the market there.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: You cannot tell by that what grade of steers were sold in the United States.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: Good slaughter steers have the same meaning in the United States as here. It is not the top limit of steers in the United States it is true, but it is the grade of steer which we market in the United States and it is $20 a hundredweight in Toronto and $19.50 on that day in Chicago.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: It does not mean a thing.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: To satisfy my hon. friend I go back to March, 1956 when the price was $17.38 in Toronto and $17.31 in Chicago. That is more nearly the same price. Then if you take the whole year 1956, the average price at Toronto was $18.80 and the average price in Chicago was $19.55. I go back over that in order to indicate that there has been no necessity for setting a floor price under cattle. The United States market is the highest market in the world for cattle. The only charge against cattle going to the United States from this country is the freight on the cattle that are shipped and a comparatively small duty which is charged against cattle going into the United States from this country.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: And the exchange.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
There is the small matter of the exchange which may be one way or the other. At present our dollar is a little bit more valuable than theirs. However, there are differences of that kind. This indicates that without any support price here at all we get practically the highest price that can be obtained from cattle anywhere in the world, and I think that is about all we can hope for.
Then we come to hogs. The yearly average for grade A hogs in 1956 at Toronto was $27.50-that is dressed weight-and in
3344	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Support Prices Chicago $20.80, a yearly average of $6.95 a hundredweight more in Canada than in the United States.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: Is that live weight?

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
That is dressed weight. Live weight is much lower than that. Then in March, 1956, the price at Toronto was $23.60 and in Chicago $17.56. In March 1957 Toronto, $30.19; Chicago, $23.33. March 30, 1957 Toronto $29.50; Chicago $24.15. Then coming down to April 5, 1957, I will give them right across Canada. Edmonton, $27.10; Winnipeg, $28; Toronto, $29.50; and Chicago, $24. In other words, at every one of those points right across the country the price was from $3.10 to $5.50 higher in Canada than the Chicago price. Those prices, of course, indicate that we have a fairly good market in Canada.
The hon. member who spoke just before me mentioned the fact I had made a speech a year ago in Winnipeg in which I called attention to the fact that there is a disease amongst the hogs in the United States which makes it impossible for them, because of the embargo we have put on, to ship hogs into this country. I warned those who were there at that time that if that disease were cleared up, and we all hope it will be, we would have difficulty maintaining a floor price of $23.
Some hon. members have indicated that all we need to do is sit down and work out a formula, apply the formula to a price and call it a parity price, then everything will be all right. Those of us who have had anything to do with these matters know that is not the case. If hogs are selling on the United States market at five or six cents a pound lower than they are here and there is no embargo because of disease, we will have so many hogs over here within a week that we will not sell any of ours. In other words, we would require to put our price down to meet their price so it would not make any difference what we thought about parity. We would be flooded out of our own market. This explains the reason why we cannot just take a formula, lay it down, and say we are going to do this. It is exactly that system that the United States tried out, under the so-called parity, and the result was they filled every cave in the United States with eggs. They had so much pork on the market that their price went down, as has been indicated here. They had so much of the other commodities on the market that their prices went down.
The only product that has not suffered that way has been wheat, and there was a special reason for that. Wheat is a commodity that you can store over a long period of time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might rise on a question of privilege. As most hon. members know, the whole debate today has been arranged by mutual consent. When it was announced by the house leader at eight o'clock that we had agreed on a vote at 9.15, it was believed the minister was within 15 or 20 minutes of the end of his speech. The arrangement was that the rest of the time was to be divided between the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny). There is not going to be much time left for them to divide if the minister has much more to say.
I realize that legally, or by the rules, he has unlimited time. He is the first minister replying to a motion of non-confidence. However, he has now spoken for about an hour and twenty minutes and I would hope he would soon conclude so the other two members to whom I referred might get at least some of the time which was arranged.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: My hon. friend understands the rules very well, and the only reason that I had to start speaking so early was that we could not get agreement on what was going to happen.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: That is not correct; agreement was reached.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
I would not have been speaking before six o'clock if agreement had been reached. I have not a great deal more to put on the record, but I do intend to put these prices on the record.
I come now to poultry products. I was going to read from this document what I had said before but I shall desist from doing that and go on to give the prices of poultry products. These are prices received by the producer in cents per dozen for eggs. In the United States in 1956 the average price received was 37.7 cents and in Canada 38.1 cents. In April, 1956, in the United States they received 32 to 36 cents in the midwest states and in Manitoba they received 35 to 37 cents. Then the current price in April, 1957, in the United States, 22 to 23 cents in the midwest states, and 30 cents in Manitoba. I shall give the spot quotations, wholesale, the price of eggs, April, 1956: New York, grade A large, 41 cents, and Montreal, 48 to 49 cents. For April, 1957: New York, 31 cents, and Montreal, 38J to 39 cents.
I come now to poultry prices. Fowl, live- well, I shall just read the 1957 prices in order to make it shorter-in Buffalo, in 1957 the price was 16 to 19 cents; in Toronto, 22 cents. Then, broilers, in Buffalo the price was 21 to 23 cents, and in Toronto 23 cents. Turkeys, live, in Buffalo, 24 cents, and in Toronto 30 cents.
Before the dinner recess, the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton) held up a sack in which they ship turkeys into this country. He was suggesting that the impression was given that they were Canadian turkeys which were in these sacks. I quite agree it would not be proper to bring them in here as American turkeys and suggest to the trade that they are a Canadian product. But here is the reason why they come in. Turkeys in the United States are 24 cents a pound; turkeys in Toronto are 30 cents a pound. They can get six cents a pound more less the duty for them by sending them into Canada, and with that difference in price, of course they will come in.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: Is 30 cents too much?

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: No, it is not too much.

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext: Why do you let them come in?

maintopic: AMENDMENT REQUESTING ESTABLISHMENT OF ADEQUATE SUPPORT PRICES
speechtext:
But they do come in over the duty.
